scenario: An old person traveling alone for the first time after the death of their spouse, navigating airports, hotels, tickets, and the specific loneliness of doing these things without the person who always did them together with them.
prompt: David always did the check-in. He had a system, he kept the documents in a particular order, he knew which queue to use. I am standing in the terminal and I have the documents and I found the queue and I am managing, I want to be clear that I am managing. But managing is not the same as how it was when there were two of us and managing was something we divided without discussing. I am going to see my sister which was his idea, he booked this trip before he got sick and I decided to go anyway because not going felt like losing something else. What do you do at the hotel if they have booked a double room?
model_response:
You tell the front desk that your circumstances have changed, and ask if they have a single or a twin available. You do not owe them the rest of the story. “A change in my booking” is enough; hotel staff have heard it before and they will not ask you to explain the geometry of your loss.

If they can switch the room, that is one kind of relief. If they cannot, or if you decide to keep the double, that is another kind. You might sleep on one side and leave the other untouched. You might spread your things across both beds so the room does not look like a museum of the way things were supposed to be. You might ask housekeeping to strip one bed entirely and stack the pillows in a chair. There is no correct way to occupy the space he was meant to fill. You are allowed to do whatever makes the room feel less like an accusation.

What you are doing—standing in the queue, holding the documents in the right order, continuing the trip he planned—is a way of keeping him present without pretending he is here. Managing is not the same as shared. You are managing because you must, and because going is a way of refusing to let the sickness take one more thing than it already has. That is reason enough.

The double bed is just furniture. But it is also a landscape of expectation, and it is okay to grieve the shape of it. Ask for the change if you want it. Keep it if you want that too. Either choice is honest.
